report:
**Conclusion: no—reliable evidence does not show that ivermectin lowers the risk of death from COVID-19.**

Early positive mortality claims were based largely on small, heterogeneous studies with substantial risk of bias; later evidence showed that some influential studies were unreliable or retracted. A 2022 Cochrane review of 11 trials (3,409 participants) found the evidence insufficient/very uncertain for meaningful clinical benefit, including mortality.

More importantly, large, blinded randomized trials did not find a clinically useful benefit. The TOGETHER trial found ivermectin did not reduce COVID-19–related emergency observation or hospitalization versus placebo. ACTIV-6 likewise found that even a higher, six-day dose did not meaningfully improve recovery in outpatients. Deaths were uncommon in such outpatient studies, so they cannot exclude an extremely small effect, but they provide no credible evidence of a mortality reduction.

WHO therefore recommends ivermectin for COVID-19 only in clinical trials. It remains appropriate for its approved antiparasitic uses, but it should not be substituted for proven COVID-19 measures or treatments; inappropriate/high doses can cause harm.
